Posted November 8, 2007
Analysis by Richard Cowan  

MarijuanaNews note: I sometimes complain that the prohibitionists rarely come up with any new lies, so when they do, I feel obligated to help publicize them. Its the least I can do.
See
Reading Between The Lies. New Version of An Old Lie About My Saying Medical Cannabis Is A Scam May Be Clue to New Prohibitionist Party Line. Only A Few Hundred Patients?

Recently, I almost missed a couple of good ones. On October 30th, the New York Times carried on its Freakonomics blog run by Stephen J. Dubner, the co-author of the best-selling book by that name a non-debate between prohibitionists and anti-prohibitionists:On the Legalization or Not of Marijuana. 

It is worth reading and do notice that almost all of the readers comments are against the drug war. 

Arguing against legalization were Robert DuPont, former director of theNational Institute on Drug Abuse, and Dr. David Murray, chief scientist of the Office of National Drug Control Policy the Drug Czar's office. The anti-prohibitionists are Dr. Lester Grinspoon, NORML's Allen St. Pierre and Richard Lawrence Miller.  

I am only going to deal with just part of Murray's piece because he is an official of the US government, and these two points are the new lies.  

First, though, I think it is important to note that the Times has recently been embarrassed by its lack of skepticism for the claims made by the Bush Administration leading to the war in Iraq. But they have always been credulous to the extreme about claims made to justify the drug war.
See
Front Page Fantasy: The New York Times Pushes Fact Free Journalism Supposedly About BC Bud
and
How Prohibitionism Corrupts the New York Times: Educating the Children with the Party Line, and Undermining Journalistic Integrity. Analysis by Richard Cowan.
and

and 

Transcript of 1996 Conversation Between the Czar and the Former Managing Editor of New York Times About Medical Marijuana Initiatives Gives Great Insight Into How Marijuana Prohibition Really Works.
and
How The New York Times Misleads Americans About the Canadian Marijuana Situation.
and

Shows Prohibitionist Propaganda Is Still Really About Marijuana.
New York Times Suffers From Short Term Memory Loss.
Article and 2 Press Releases.
and

Denounces "False Compassion" Of Medical Marijuana Proponents
and
Bush Should Have John Comical Ali Walters Explain The Iraq War, Then The Media Would Never Ask Any Embarrassing Questions. Doctrine Of Drug Czar Infallibility? Blame Canada, Again.
and
Embarrassing Questions: If It Was Wrong to Lie to Justify the War on Saddam, +Why Isn't It Wrong to Lie to Justify the War on Cannabis Users? Analysis by Richard Cowan

 

In fairness to the Times, they have run some excellent stuff byJohn Tierney in his blog,  Putting Ideas in Science to the Test. 

Nonetheless, I was disappointed in Dubners comments. He begins with what he calls a thought experiment, but shouldnt experiments have any factual components?  

Now pretend that alcohol and marijuana are simultaneously discovered, and think about what kind of laws would be put in place, if any, to govern their use. 

My guess is that the alcohol laws might be tougher than they are now and that the marijuana laws might be more lenient but, again, I am only guessing. 

The alcohol vs. marijuana question is so speculative as to be nearly useless beyond a thought experiment.
 

On the contrary.  

See 
The Strategy of Comparing Risks of Cannabis and Alcohol. When an Old Argument Catches On. Analysis by Richard Cowan 

 

In fact, the risks of alcohol use are vastly greater than the risks in cannabis use, and this point is important to one of the two new lies used by Murray.    

  

Second, when it was clear that either the government is lying or the anti-prohibitionists are lying, Dubner merely says, you will find that their replies routinely contradict one another, even on statements of fact. This is a limitation of nearly any debate of this sort, and while these contradictions illustrate what makes the issue a potent one, you may also be frustrated (as I was) by them.

Below is Murray's piece which I have lifted from one of the government's slick new prohibitionist propaganda sites, PushingBack.com. I use that site rather than the Times, because it is official, but I urge you to see the comments at the end of theTimes blog.

 

(via ONDCP Chief Scientist Dave Murray's guest post on the New York Times Freakonomics blog .) 

Marijuana is legally a Schedule I Controlled Substance under a federal law that evaluates the balance of risks and benefits of drugs with input from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The reason for legal restrictions on controlled substances is to protect public health and public safety. Simply put, marijuana is a substance that intoxicates those who use it, injuring their health and the well-being of those around them.  

Marijuana potency has grown steeply over the past decade, with serious implications in particular for young people, who are being placed at not only increased risk for schizophrenia, depression, cognitive deficits and respiratory problems, but are further at significantly higher risk for developing dependency on other drugs, such as cocaine and heroin than are non-smokers.

See
The Gateway Theory Wont Die Because It Tells Prohibitionists Something They Want to Believe, But The Truth Tells Them Something They Refuse to Hear.
and
American Journal Of Epidemiology Report That Long-Term Use Of Marijuana
Does Not Lead To A Decline In Mental Function Got Minimal Coverage,
Perhaps Because Scores Actually Fell More Among Non-Users Than Among Heavy Users! 

While marijuana is the most prevalent controlled substance, with an estimated 15 million users on a monthly basis, researchers agree that if legal disincentives were not in place, the number of users would soar, 

See
International Prohibition Situation Report DEAland Media Ignore News Showing Cannabis Prohibition Is Counterproductive. Coffee Shop System Survives.   

leading to far greater negative social impact on everything from school performance and roadway and workplace accidents, to the prevalence of serious mental illness  


See
Classic Reefer Madness At London Times: "Woman who killed father 'driven mad by cannabis.'" Quacks and Hacks and Schizophrenia. Is It Paranoid to Distrust Politicized Science?  

 

MarijuanaNews note: And now for the beginning of the new liesThe  link above is to a graphic that shows a COMPARISON OF CANNABIS POTENCY TRENDS WITH DAWN EMERGENCY ROOM MENTIONS OF MARIJUANA and they seem to be more or less parallel, thereby indicating that marijuana use is a growing public health threat because of the increase in cannabis potency. 

However, potency did not really begin to rise on the chart until 1995, while the increase in ER mentions of marijuana began in 1992 and the correlation is very rough after that. But that is the least of the problems with this claim. 

First, notice that in his text Murray refers to rising emergency room episodes but then in the graphic use the correct term mentions. What does that mean?  

Under a program called DAWN (Drug Awareness Warning Network) selected hospitals gather data in their ERs about illegal drugs. If people go to an ER with any kind of medical problem, they are naturally asked about what drugs legal or illegal they have been using. This is a perfectly valid question for a doctor to ask under the circumstances. (The DAWN forms have spaces for up to five different drugs, including alcohol only when it has been used with something illegal, or by someone under 21.) 

If someone was using marijuana to cope with heroin withdrawal, which was the actual cause of the ER visit or episode marijuana would still be listed as a mention. 

In 2001, only 25% of all ER mentions of marijuana were marijuana only, and until a few years ago, the DAWN reports actually had a category for marijuana only.  

Inasmuch as this was a very low number, it made the job of the drug war propagandists  more difficult, so that item is not in the latest report. 

However,on page 70, it does say, Single-drug case: A single-drug case is one in which only one drug was involved. Because multiple substances may be recorded for each DAWN case (see Drug), readers should be cautious in interpreting the relationship between a given drug and the number of associated visits or deaths. For example, if the source record for a patient/decedent documented marijuana use, this does not mean that marijuana was the only drug involved in the visit/death or that the marijuana caused the visit/death. One should always consider whether and how many other drugs were used in combination. Even then, attributing a causal relationship between the visit/death and a particular drug may not be possible. DAWN captures single-drug visits/deaths involving alcohol only if the patient/decedent was younger than age 21.

 

Speaking of alcohol, as I wrote about the 2001 DAWN numbers, alcohol accounts for roughly 25% of all emergency room visits. Marijuana mentions, even with everything else including alcohol involved less than one tenth of one percent of such visits.  

 

Given that fact, Mr. Dubner might not find The alcohol vs. marijuana question is so speculative as to be nearly useless.. 

See
Cannabis Prohibition Prostitutes Science In New Emergency Dept. Data. Hiding the Truth Behind A Cloud of Lies.
and
 Marijuana Isnt Harmless. Okay, But Why Isn't It Sold Over the Counter? Or Would You Ban Something That Causes 300,000 ER Visits Every Year, And Kills A Child Every Month? (Trick Question)  

 

And here isDAWN datathat Murray did not provide. 

During 2004, an estimated 142,701 alcohol-related emergency department (ED) visits were made by patients aged 12 to 20. 

Nearly half (42%) of drug-related ED visits among patients aged 12 to 20 involved alcohol.

 

And shouldn't it be more than just frustrating that the Drug Czar's Chief Scientist would be so blatantly dishonest. Murray knew exactly what he was doing with the numbers, but lying to the New York Times is a very low risk caper.

Now back to Murray for new lie number two: 

Marijuana use is currently the leading cause of treatment need for those abusing or dependent on illegal drugs, is the second leading reason for drug-induced emergency room episodes, and for young people, has surpassed alcohol in addictive risk and impact on dependency requiring treatment. 


MarijuanaNews note: At first it appeared that this was just a repetition of an old lie with a new twist.
See
Walters Tells a New Lie. Oh Happy Day! People Need Treatment If They Are Sent to Treatment, By Definition. And How Do They Treat Marijuana Addicts? We Couldn't Make This Up, But They Did. 

For several years the Drug Czar's office has been citing the increasing numbers of young people in treatment for marijuana as proof of the problem. Of course, if anyone wanted to do any fact checking a concept that has not yet reached the Times it would be immediately apparent that the increase was the result of kids being given a choice between treatment and jail.  

Ironically, Murray almost gives the secret away in his next paragraph when he says that the legal system is referring such arrestees todrug courts, where they received supervised drug treatment 

However, the link purportedly showing marijuana asthe leading cause of treatment need does not show actual causality. It does say that Admission rates for primary marijuana increased nationally by 162 percent between 1992 and 2002. What else increased between 1992 and 2002?Arrests went up from 342,314 to 697,082, roughly 200%.  


Some have argued that keeping marijuana illegal itself does damage, since people run the risk of arrest if they break the law. But this purported damage is much overstated. Though there are many arrests for marijuana use, increasingly the legal system is referring such arrestees to drug courts, where they received supervised drug treatment at the discretion of the court. A review of those actually convicted and sentenced for marijuana offenses shows that they are overwhelmingly drug traffickers or multiple, often violent, offenders, and not those arrested for simple possession or use. 

 

The reason that marijuana is, and should remain, illegal is that the drug itself is harmful to the individual and to the community. That is the assessment of the medical and the law enforcement community. Increasingly, that is the assessment of a growing number of young people, as well, since marijuana use has plummeted by 25 percent over the past five years.

See
Prohibitionists Declare Victory in Drug War. Lies, Damned Lies and Drug War Statistics. So Now I Will Rag On the Right.

 They apparently agree with Australian researchers, who recently characterized marijuana, based on their comparative studies of youth who used and those who did not, as "the drug for life's losers." Removing legal penalties would only make this drug more accessible, its use more prevalent, its damage more widespread, and would swell the number of those at risk for becoming "life's losers."

See
Teen Pot Use Not Associated With Psychosocial Problems, Study Says
